The study contributes to research on business model innovation (BMI) and the sharing economy literature by showing that BMI in SPSMEs is not a one-off design outcome. Rather, it is an evolving and context-sensitive process shaped by firm-level adaptation and business ecosystem conditions, particularly in developing economies.

title: A review on blockchain-driven e-healthcare service user empowerment
From creative output to creative governance: Legitimizing AI-generated creativity under deepfake uncertainty
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence challenges established foundations of innovation legitimacy by decoupling output quality from human effort, intention, and responsibility. When creative outputs no longer provide reliable signals of human agency, legitimacy judgments must be reconstructed through alternative interpretive cues. This study reconceptualizes innovation legitimacy as an inferential process formed under conditions of technological opacity and examines how governance practices shape legitimacy judgments in AI-mediated creativity. Drawing on a survey-based experiment (N = 240), we investigate how configurations of AI involvement, transparency timing, and deepfake-related manipulation cues influence perceived deception, perceived human effort, and perceived authenticity. Legitimacy judgments, operationalized as inferential assessments of deception, effort, and authenticity, are distinguished from their downstream attitudinal and behavioral consequences. The findings show that legitimacy in AI-mediated creativity shifts from output-based evaluation toward governance-dependent sensemaking. Transparency operates as an interpretive mechanism whose effects depend critically on timing, while deepfake cues systematically heighten moral uncertainty and undermine legitimacy. By specifying the microfoundations through which legitimacy breaks down and is partially reconstructed under AI-induced opacity, the study advances innovation theory by reframing legitimacy as a governance-dependent inferential achievement. This reframing differs from existing interpretive and institutional accounts: governance is conceptualized not as a mechanism that generates legitimacy directly through compliance or ceremonial conformity, but as an interpretive infrastructure that shapes the conditions under which audiences can form legitimacy judgments when conventional output-based cues are absent. The findings contribute to debates on AI governance, innovation diffusion, and responsible innovation in contexts characterized by ambiguous agency and uncertainty about algorithmic production processes.

title: Frugal business models: A systemic perspective from the international literature
Institutionalizing portfolio entrepreneurship: the Venture Studio model
abstract: Venture Studios (VSs) are organizations that create start-ups by acting as founders or co-founders and operating through standardized venture creation processes conducted in parallel. To examine this organizational model and delineate its distinctiveness from others, we developed a global database, conducted multiple case studies with twelve European VSs and two international networks, and administered a worldwide survey. Drawing on human capital and organizational learning perspectives, this study identifies the architectural characteristics and mechanisms through which VSs institutionalize portfolio entrepreneurship. Our findings reveal how VSs convert individual entrepreneurial expertise into organizationally codified human capital. In doing so, VSs extend entrepreneurial agency and cognition from individuals to organizations, offering an organizational model for parallel venture creation. Finally, we clarify how VSs complement other entrepreneurial actors by reducing early-stage uncertainty and generating validated, investment-ready ventures.

title: Resource orchestration in incubator management: Evidence from multiple cases
abstract: Incubators play a vital role in entrepreneurial ecosystems by providing start-ups with resources such as funding, mentorship, and access to networks. Incubator systems differ from traditional organizations because start-ups remain legally and strategically independent, which limits hierarchical control and makes coordination inherently relational. However, existing research tends to emphasize the effects of individual resources, paying less attention to how incubators orchestrate resources through ongoing interaction with ventures, leaving unresolved why incubators with similar resource bases often produce markedly different outcomes. Thus, drawing on Resource Orchestration Theory, this study examines how incubators structure, bundle, and leverage resources, and how orchestration operates across multiple levels to shape start-up growth and incubator performance. Based on a qualitative multi-case study, we identify a four-stage cyclical orchestration process in which incubators (1) structure a foundational resource base, (2) provide tailored initial resource packages, (3) dynamically reconfigure bundled resources as ventures evolve, and (4) activate start-up feedback. Feedback takes concrete forms such as alumni mentoring, network bridging, investment connections, and reputational endorsements, which replenish the incubator's resource base and enable subsequent rounds of support. We further theorize a multi-level mechanism comprising incubator orchestration, start-up orchestration, and joint orchestration; joint orchestration operates through coordinated resource acquisition, bundling, and leveraging, helping explain outcome heterogeneity beyond resource stock differences.

title: How does digital transformation and Global Innovation Network Embedding affect ESG performance of multinational enterprises? Empirical evidence from an Eastern innovation pattern
abstract: As an important manifestation of data-driven technological innovation paradigms, digital transformation has become a key pathway through which multinational enterprises reshape their innovation processes, enhance global competitiveness, and achieve sustainable value creation. It not only transforms firms’ modes of knowledge creation, organizational coordination mechanisms, and resource allocation logic, but also creates new opportunities for multinational enterprises to deepen their global innovation network embedding and improve ESG performance. However, existing studies have rarely systematically explored the impact mechanism of digital transformation on ESG performance from the perspective of global innovation network embedding. Grounded in the resource-based theory and social network theory, using panel data of Chinese A-share listed multinational enterprises from 2010 to 2022, the impact and mechanism of digital transformation on ESG performance in multinational enterprises were empirically analyzed by employing the two-way fixed effects model, the mediation effect model and the moderation effect model. Results indicate that, (1) Digital transformation has a significantly positive effect on the ESG performance. (2) The mechanism through which digital transformation enhances ESG performance lies in accelerating the global innovation network embedding of multinational enterprises. (3) Internal control quality strengthens the positive effect of digital transformation on ESG performance, whereas external environmental uncertainty weakens this effect. (4) The digital transformation has a stronger incentive effect on ESG performance for large-scale, manufacturing, and technology and labor-intensive multinational enterprises. The obtained conclusions contribute to fully leveraging the driving effect of digital transformation by multinational enterprises in the global value chain and provide empirical evidence that such firms can enhance their global collaborative innovation capability and sustainable competitive advantage through digital transformation.

title: PATTERN-X: Guiding sustainable innovation in intelligent lighting systems through an explainable AI framework for technology convergence forecasting
The effects of generative AI usage on employee innovation: Collaboration modes, idea journey, and decline in creative psychological ownership
The designer's turn: Reconfiguring professional identity for project innovation in the generative AI era
Exploratory versus exploitative innovation in central state-owned enterprises: the role of administrative rank
Configuring hybrid agency: How both technological agency and human agency drive blockchain-based risk mitigation
Editorial Board
Using leverage points to identify interventions for transitioning the Dutch road infrastructure sector toward sustainability
abstract: The transition toward sustainability in infrastructure sectors requires interventions that address systemic lock-ins rather than isolated technological improvements. However, innovation ecosystem research offers only limited guidance on how public-sector-driven ecosystems can be intentionally steered toward sustainability under conditions of structural inertia. This study employs Donella Meadows’ leverage points framework to identify and categorize potential systemic interventions in the Dutch road infrastructure innovation ecosystem. Using an action-oriented research design conducted over 1.5 years with public clients, contractors, and knowledge institutions, the study identifies 25 interventions across five thematic areas. The findings show that interventions predominantly target system design and feedback structures, the strengthening of governance, foresight, and integration capabilities rather than focusing on parameter-level change. This highlights how transformations in public-sector innovation ecosystems emerge through the gradual reconfiguration of rules, information flows, and coordination mechanisms. The study contributes to innovation ecosystem research by demonstrating how leverage points can be used to guide and structure ecosystem-level intervention strategies and support deliberate steering of public-sector-driven innovation ecosystems toward sustainability.

title: Mapping urban-industrial symbiosis through a business ecosystem lens
abstract: This paper examines the evolution of urban industrial symbiosis (UIS) through a business ecosystem lens. UIS, defined as the synergistic integration of urban and industrial systems where waste and by-products are repurposed as industrial inputs, has demonstrated strong potential to address climate change, urbanization challenges, and supply chain vulnerabilities. Existing UIS research has primarily focused on material flows, network structures, and policy arrangements. However, limited attention has been paid to how coordination mechanisms evolve as ecosystem interdependence and complexity increase over time. This omission is consequential because even powerful coordinators face structural limits when coordinating expanding interdependencies among heterogeneous actors and resource flows, creating a coordination gap. Drawing on case studies of Ulsan (South Korea), Händelö (Sweden), EcoPark (Hong Kong), Metro Vancouver (Canada), Kalundborg (Denmark), HS Orka (Iceland), and Kawasaki (Japan), the paper develops a process model of UIS ecosystem coordination that links generation-processing-auxiliary (G-P-A) subsystems, coordination tensions and mechanisms, and governance pathways across three analytical phases. The study advances UIS research by shifting from exchange-oriented perspectives toward dynamic ecosystem coordination and theorizing how coordination mechanisms evolve under increasing ecosystem complexity. It further extends business ecosystem theory by explaining how increasingly distributed coordination capacity sustains ecosystem resilience as growing interdependence strains centralized orchestration.

title: Artificial intelligence anxiety among creative professionals: Evidence from the Brazilian creative economy
Artificial intelligence and supply chain resilience: The roles of knowledge-based dynamic capabilities and digital leadership
abstract: Amid growing global uncertainty and supply chain disruptions, strengthening supply chain resilience has emerged as a key strategic priority for firms. Although artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionising supply chain management, existing research lacks an understanding of the impacts of firm-level AI adoption on supply chain resilience, particularly through capability-building mechanisms. Drawing on knowledge-based dynamic capabilities theory and socio-technical systems theory, this paper constructs a theoretical framework to explain how firm-level AI adoption enhances supply chain resilience. Applying panel data from 3,252 Chinese A-share listed firms over the period 2010-2023, our findings reveal that AI adoption positively strengthens supply chain resilience. Mechanism analyses indicate that absorptive capability and innovative capability serve as significant mediators of this relationship, whereas adaptive capability does not. Moreover, top executives’ digital leadership positively moderates the AI adoption—supply chain resilience nexus. Further heterogeneity analysis shows that effects are relatively pronounced in non-state-owned enterprises, technology-intensive/non-manufacturing industries, and developed, highly marketized regions. These findings advance understanding of the mechanism whereby AI adoption fosters supply chain resilience through capability development and highlight digital leadership as a vital enabler in AI-driven digital transformation.

title: Digital transformation and innovation resilience under geopolitical conflict: Evidence from U.S.-China technology sanctions
Leveraging IoT for business model innovation in banking: The role of data-driven decision-making, Fintech innovation and artificial intelligence
Internal and external design integration, launch strategy proficiency, and new product development performance: The contingent role of market dynamism
abstract: Design capabilities have been recognized as drivers of innovation, yet the distinction between internal and external design integration remains largely underexplored, as do the ways through which these integration types contribute to new product development (NPD) performance. Drawing on the dynamic knowledge management view, this study conceptualizes internal and external design integration as distinct loci of market-facing knowledge generation that are associated with launch strategy proficiency and, in turn, with NPD performance. Survey data from 247 U.S. firms show an indirect association between both types of design integration and NPD performance through launch strategy proficiency. Market dynamism reveals a capability reversal. Under stable market conditions, internal design integration is positively associated with launch strategy proficiency, whereas external design integration becomes negatively associated with it at very low levels of dynamism. Under dynamic market conditions, external design integration is positively associated with launch strategy proficiency, whereas the association between internal design integration and launch strategy proficiency is attenuated. The findings connect the design and marketing research streams and offer guidance for decision-makers on aligning the locus of design integration with the level of market dynamism.

title: How digital platform capability builds competitive advantage in platform firms: The mediating role of intrapreneurship and user value co-creation
Balancing human and artificial creativity: A paradox perspective on artistic production in the GenAI era
abstract: The relationship between creativity and artificial intelligence (AI) has attracted widespread attention from the public, corporations, and academia. Advanced AI-based examples of artistic production, such as AI generated music, poetry, and paintings, have started transforming the creative and cultural industries. This study analyzed the componential model of creativity through the lens of the Generative AI (GenAI) artwork produced by artists. A qualitative approach was employed utilizing data collected from interviews with various artists, critics, and technicians who worked with GenAI, thereby helping in identifying the creativity paradoxes in the AI era. The results suggest that the use of GenAI has created dualities in the components of creativity, including tensions between extrinsic and intrinsic motivations, artistic and technical skills, and creations by an artist and those generated by AI. Given that AI will continue to develop, the cultural and creative industries need to find ways to navigate these creativity paradoxes.

title: Source of novelty and invention impact: Evidence from biotechnology patents
From functional connectivity to human-machine empathy: Scene value co-creation driven by GenAI-enabled smart elderly care based on a hybrid agency perspective
Governance and innovation in higher education: The moderating role of vice-chancellors’ professional characteristics
Impact of supply chain digital transformation orientation alignment on corporate green innovation: An extended resource-based view perspective
Ambidextrous innovation leap and patent abandonment: A resource orchestration perspective
Design longevity: Institutional lock-in and the Toyota Crown Comfort taxi
abstract: While product design is a key driver of organizational success, companies increasingly struggle to sustain relevance in markets with ever-shortening product lifecycles. This study investigates how products achieve longevity without frequent redesign. A historical analysis of the Toyota Crown Comfort taxi, which remained in production for approximately 23-years (1995–2018), is used as a case to examine institutional lock-in as a complementary explanation for design longevity. The results identify three interrelated institutional mechanisms operating at the government-, industry-, and consumer-levels that collectively reinforced the vehicle's enduring market position. Building on these findings, the study proposes a conceptual framework demonstrating how institutional ecosystems can sustain dominant product designs over time. The research contributes to the product design, timeless design, and institutional lock-in literatures by demonstrating that long-term institutional relationships may provide an alternative pathway to design longevity beyond continuous redesign and R&D investment.

title: Beyond the efficiency trap: Regional AI exposure, AI knowledge, and the asymmetric governance of data-driven value propositions
Divide Et Impera: Structuring design science projects
abstract: Design Science (DS) has attracted growing interest in entrepreneurship and innovation research in recent years. Typically implemented through projects, DS projects are often complex and challenging to manage. This study explores how DS projects can be effectively structured to support several tasks for DS project management particularly regarding the division of research tasks and the allocation of project resources. We present a framework that segments the content of DS projects into small, well-defined, and individually manageable research components. The framework enables researchers to assign resources strategically, assess the balance of research output, schedule and monitor activities systematically, and adapt to changes in scope and objectives during project execution. To illustrate the framework's practical utility, we draw on a case study involving the development of an innovative blockchain-based solution for VAT settlement in Denmark. Additionally, we evaluated the framework's general applicability by comparing it against ten DS projects described in the scientific literature. This is complemented with a discussion of how the framework can be embedded into the DS project management process according to established projects management standards. The evaluation results support our claims about the framework's broader applicability and its potential to improve DS project management.

title: How team structure shapes technological differentiation: A semantic embedding-based assessment
abstract: A firm's research portfolio often faces a tension between reliance on dominant technologies and the pursuit of technological differentiation. This study examines how invention teams generate such differentiation by linking network structure to innovation outcomes. We develop a novel semantic distance measure based on patent text, capturing technological differentiation along a continuous space rather than discrete classification categories. Using this measure, we show that invention teams achieve higher levels of differentiation when they combine strong internal cohesion with diverse external network connections. Specifically, cohesive internal ties facilitate knowledge integration, while external ties spanning structural holes expand access to novel knowledge. These findings highlight the importance of balancing cohesion and brokerage in shaping technological differentiation and offer new insights into the organization of inventive activity.

title: Pursuing technology sovereignty under dependency: The case of Mistral AI
abstract: This study examines how organizations pursue technological sovereignty while embedded in infrastructures controlled by geopolitical competitors. We address this question through an in-depth longitudinal case study of Mistral AI (2023–2025), Europe's only frontier-scale Large Language Model developer competing with American incumbents. Our analysis draws on two primary data sources collected over the firm's first three years: 16 media interviews with CEO Arthur Mensch and 30 monthly activity reports published by Mistral, triangulated with technical documentation, industry analyses, and European policy documents. We employed an abductive analytical approach, combining iterative open and focused coding of institutional work practices with theoretical dimensioning and process tracing across four temporal phases of the company's evolution. Our findings reveal three interrelated forms of institutional work: selective decoupling of critical dependencies while maintaining beneficial connections, strategic leveraging of embeddedness in some structures to contest dominance in others, and structural reconfiguration creating alternative institutional arrangements. These practices constitute geopolitical embedded agency, a distinctive form of organizational action characterized by material rather than symbolic embeddedness; cross-scalar institutional contradictions; and sovereignty objectives that reshape conventional organizational rationality. Our framework contributes to institutional work theory and emerging technology sovereignty scholarship while extending analytically to other capital-intensive sectors facing geopolitical dependencies.

title: Reimagining work in ageing societies: AI-enabled reskilling and the power of future work identities
Corporate innovation propensity: From measurement to impact—A text-based analytical approach
From threat to reconfiguration: How content creators reshape occupational identity in AI-driven creative practices
From policy to practice: Translating mission-oriented innovation policy into responsible innovation governance and employee behavioral outcomes
Artificial intelligence at the intersection of innovation and marketing: A conceptual model and research propositions
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the theory and practice of innovation and marketing, yet its deployment at their intersection remains only partially understood. Existing literature has not thoroughly examined which AI capabilities (analytical, generative) are more appropriate during different stages of the new product development (NPD) process, how a core marketing factor, customer involvement, conditions the outcomes of these capabilities, or how AI-related risks and governance mechanisms shape NPD performance across stages. This study addresses these gaps by proposing a novel conceptual framework that links the two distinct AI capability types to specific NPD stages, examines how customer involvement moderates the relationship between AI capabilities and NPD outcomes, integrates AI hallucination risk as a formal boundary condition differentiating the failure modes of AI capabilities across stages, and extends the framework to NPD governance mechanisms including gate evaluations, feedback loops, and cross-functional coordination. The paper contributes to research and practice by (1) offering a set of propositions regarding AI’s role at the intersection of innovation and marketing, (2) providing theoretically derived guidance for managers on deploying AI capabilities during NPD while recognizing the marketing imperative of customer involvement, and (3) outlining a future research agenda on AI-enabled innovation which is of crucial importance for the future of business. Collectively, the paper advances a more theoretically rigorous and practically relevant understanding of AI’s transformative role in innovation and marketing.

title: AI capability and product innovation intensity: Driving B2B marketing innovation under varying levels of market turbulence
From AI potential to sustainable value: The AI-SDGs value cycle as an integrative framework for sustainable innovation
Governing sustainable co-creation in business–NGO collaborations: Institutional logics and innovation outcomes
abstract: This study examines how governance in business-NGO collaborations conditions co-creation for sustainable innovation under institutional plurality. Drawing on institutional logics theory, we conduct a qualitative cross-case study of five Scandinavian retail firms and their NGO partners. We identify three recurrent governance configurations: separated coexistence, assimilated coexistence, and logic blending. The configurations differ in how partners manage organizational boundaries, allocate decision authority, integrate knowledge, and establish accountability. In the cases studied, separated coexistence was recurrently associated with regulative innovation, where protected organizational distance supported credible monitoring and verification. Assimilated coexistence was recurrently associated with inclusive sustainable business innovation, where NGO knowledge entered bounded parts of firm-led innovation. Logic blending was most evident in social impact innovation, where joint problem framing, shared interpretation of evidence, and relational accountability supported long-term societal outcomes. These relationships represent empirical tendencies rather than necessary, sufficient, or exclusive associations. Different configurations may coexist across activities and may evolve as collaborations mature. The study extends institutional logics research by showing how responses to plurality are operationalized as interorganizational governance arrangements that structure decision rights, knowledge interfaces, boundaries, and accountability. It contributes to sustainable co-creation research by explaining why different innovation tasks call for different combinations of governance practices.

title: When digital meets green: How technological convergence drives eco-innovation in Chinese firms
Building sustainable futures: The micro-foundational dynamics behind energy community ecosystem
abstract: Energy Communities (ECs) are increasingly recognized as collaborative ecosystems that support energy transition. However, existing research has predominantly explained their emergence from macro- and meso-level perspectives, offering limited insight into micro-level mechanisms. Although broader ecosystem research has only recently begun to explain ecosystem-level outcomes from a micro-level perspective, treating individuals as the primary unit of analysis, it has paid limited attention to the relational mechanisms through which individual actions and interactions contribute to ecosystem emergence. To address this gap, this study adopts a microfoundational perspective to examine the creation and development of an energy community ecosystem through an in-depth qualitative case study conducted in Southern Italy. Drawing on semi-structured interviews triangulated with multiple documentary sources analyzed through Reflexive Thematic Analysis, the findings identify three relational microfoundational mechanisms, namely micro-level collaborative initiatives, micro-relational engagement toward cultural change, and relation-driven energy inclusion that explain how energy community ecosystems progressively emerge from individual actions and interactions across the ideation, formalization, and growth phases. The study advances the explanatory capacity of the microfoundational perspective by extending its application to energy community ecosystems, providing actionable insights for designing inclusive, context-sensitive interventions tailored to different phases of ecosystem development.

title: Engagement in innovation ecosystems and commercialization of innovation: geography of collaboration, uncertainty and risk
Looking back, thinking ahead: A systematic review of business models in SMEs
abstract: Business Models (BMs) are central to how SMEs compete in dynamic environments. Despite their importance, research on BMs in SMEs remains fragmented, with limited integration across theoretical perspectives and empirical insights. This study addresses that gap through a systematic literature review of 405 articles retrieved from Scopus and WoS, mapping the intellectual structure of BMs research in SMEs. Using bibliometric and thematic analysis, six dominant research clusters are identified and synthesised. Drawing on key theories, including the resource-based view, dynamic capabilities, and stakeholder theory, the study develops an integrative framework linking contextual determinants, configuration mechanisms, and the strategic, operational, and societal outcomes of BMs in SMEs. The framework positions BMs in SMEs as context-sensitive systems shaped by the interplay of resources, adaptive capabilities, and stakeholder expectations. The paper concludes with a future research agenda that highlights overlooked areas, including how SMEs navigate overlapping pressures, internal heterogeneity, micro-level BM processes, responsible digital practices, and diverse network structures. By integrating fragmented insights into a coherent framework, this review provides a foundation for advancing theory and offering practical guidance for SMEs operating under resource constraints and environmental turbulence.

title: Technology adoption among silver tourists: A cross-cultural configurational comparison of Greece and the United Kingdom
abstract: Silver tourism is a rapidly growing segment of global tourism, yet older adults face persistent digital divides when engaging with smart travel platforms. This study examines technology use intentions among 800 silver tourists in Greece (Athens) and the UK (Birmingham) through a complexity-informed bounded Rational Choice Theory framework. Integrating fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) with Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA), the study identifies sufficient configurations of six conditions namely perceived usefulness, ease of use, subjective norms, cognition, trust, and perceived competence alongside city-specific necessary conditions. Subjective norms emerge as necessary in Athens (collectivist, digitally uneven), while trust and perceived competence are necessary in Birmingham (individualist, digitally mature). In total, the analysis identified three acceptable pathways: one shared pathway, the Cognitive-Competence users which was valid in both Greek and British contexts, and two context-specific pathways, namely the Usage-Norm Consumers in Greece and the Cognitive Trust-in-Competence users in the UK. Post-evaluation interviews with six tourism managers confirmed the ecological validity of the identified pathways and strengthened the practical relevance of the findings. Findings extend digital divide theory, Rational Choice Theory, and complexity theory, offering culturally tailored guidance for inclusive tourism technology design.

title: Antecedents of growth hacking in small and medium-sized enterprises: A technology-organization-environment perspective in developing economies
Navigating personal control: AI augmentation and its impact on decision-making
abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in organizational decision-making, it fundamentally reshapes workers' perceptions of agency and influence. While AI augmentation is often promoted as a way to preserve human autonomy, empirical evidence regarding its psychological consequences remains fragmented. This study adopts Control Theory to examine how different levels of AI involvement affect perceived Personal Control (PC). Through an online within-subject experiment (N=124), participants performed a logistical optimization task (bin-packing) under varying degrees of AI support. Findings reveal that high AI involvement significantly reduces PC, whereas low and medium levels maintain PC at levels comparable to the no-AI baseline. The research identifies perceived responsibility as a key mediator: increased AI intervention diminishes the sense of responsibility, subsequently eroding PC. Furthermore, the user’s personality, specifically Locus of Control, moderates this relationship, suggesting that individuals with an internal orientation are more sensitive to control loss. The study highlights a "critical threshold" beyond which technological integration becomes counterproductive for human agency, offering practical implications for the design of human-centric AI systems in the workplace.

title: Developing a maturity model for circular economy transitions: A firm-level artifact grounded in design science
abstract: Many firms facing major regulatory, resource, and market challenges are increasingly under pressure to adopt circular economy practices, yet they lack integrated and empirically validated tools to evaluate their circular maturity in a systemic and actionable way. To fill this gap, our study developed the Circular Maturity Tool (CMT), an artifact that assesses firms' circular capabilities and guides capability development across successive stages. Using a design science (DS) approach, we conceptualize circular maturity as a capability comprising interdependent organizational dimensions that the CMT integrates in a staged architecture. Following a full DS cycle, the CMT is grounded in a systematic literature review and 54 interviews, that we then refined through expert-based alpha testing, and subsequently tested in a multi-method beta evaluation. Guided by the Design Science Validity Framework, the evaluation confirmed the CMT's structural integrity and contextual robustness and revealed positive associations between maturity scores and the adoption of circular resource strategies. The study contributes to science by specifying an integrated developmental logic that links organizational dimensions, maturity levels, and operationalized capabilities, and by demonstrating how DS supports rigorous artifact development and evaluation. In practice, the CMT helps firms assess their circular maturity, identify capability gaps, benchmark progress, and prioritize capability development; to date, it has been applied in nearly 3000 assessments across more than 900 firms.
